description: Designing a game to run a Martian Outpost.
summary: Odyssey Zero is an interactive game that teaches young players the value of  decision-making is when it comes to keeping a colony on Mars alive. Each day brings a new challenge based on NASA's weather data, requiring players to make decisions about energy and resource management. But there's a catch: a decision of what might seem good for the colony one day can prove to be detrimental the next. Players must think ahead, adapt to changing conditions, and consider how their choices affect the colony in the long run. By combining real NASA data with interactive gameplay, Odyssey Zero makes learning about space exploration, sustainability, and problem-solving more engaging. The goal is to help young players understand the challenges of living on Mars while encouraging them to think critically and make thoughtful decisions.
details:
Odyssey Zero is a survival game that runs in a web browser and is set on Mars. Players look after a small base one day at a time and try to last as long as they can, picking crops in the greenhouse, checking the solar panels, refilling the oxygen tank, cooking meals, and going to bed. Challenges may arise: A solar flare gives the player seconds to get inside. A coronal mass ejection (CME) gives them about a minute to pick ripe crops, get indoors, and shut down the solar panels before they are damaged. A dust storm blocks the light, buries the panels, and shakes the greenhouse apart if it isn't repaired. Every choice has a cost: stopping the panels protects them but drains stored energy quickly, so the player is always trading safety against power. When they get it wrong, they see it in sparking power cords, smoking panels, and withered plants.

The flares and CMEs in the game are not invented. The game pulls records from NASA's DONKI space weather database, including the flare class, the CME speed, and the active region on the Sun each one came from, and it uses those facts to decide how much warning the player gets. A stronger flare or a faster CME means less time to react. If the live data can't be reached, the game falls back on an archived record and labels it as such, so players always know what they are looking at. Daily science facts from NASA's Open Science Data Repository appear during play, and the dust shield is based on NASA's research into electrodynamic dust shields. After every emergency, a "What really happened" screen explains the science behind what the player just went through. When the mission ends, a debrief explains what real mission planners learn from that kind of failure. A Trainer Guide, a glossary, and a visual How to Play screen with arrows pointing at the actual game scenes are built in as well.

The aim is for players to come away understanding something that is easy to overlook: power, air and food are all connected, and real crews shelter early because the warning time is short. The learning comes from decisions rather than reading, because the player is the one who loses a crop or a panel when they hesitate. The game is creative in how everyday chores set up the danger. The player is already low on time, hungry, or short on power when an alert goes off, so tensions can certainly affect one’s decisions making ability. A small NASA-style weather app built into the game shows tasks, weather and warnings, so the information comes from inside the world the player is standing in.

The game was built with plain JavaScript and the HTML5 canvas, with no game engine or outside libraries, so it runs in any modern browser with nothing to install. It uses the NASA DONKI web API for live data, saved in the browser for six hours so it doesn't keep asking, and pixel-art images for the map, house, greenhouse, crops and character. The team weighed several factors along the way. Timers, energy drain and how fast food rots are simplified so the game is fun, while the event types, flare classes and explanations come from NASA sources. New players are guided by prompts like "Refill oxygen (E)" when they stand near something usable, and a checklist during each emergency crosses off finished steps. The status bars collapse into a drop-down because they were covering the objects players needed to interact with. The game is also fair, since crops can't be picked before they are ripe, alerts pause the game while they are read, and urgent warnings stay visible even when the status bar is hidden. It keeps working even if NASA's service is down.
